sweep.title: The console on the lanes' measured throughput, on a VCE-like peak day harder than planned
sweep.description: Does the console recommend better lanes on a day slower than planned when it measures the lanes' throughput from the day (S22.5) instead of reading the checkpoint's settings, made for the plan (ADR-059)? The plan and GateFlow's settings assume a screening time of 24 seconds per person. Today's practice with staff calls (fifo-manual) runs with the plan only, with a supervisor who opens a lane when the queue is long (@reactive), with the console on the settings (@advise) and on the measured throughput (@advise-measured); GateFlow's priority calls (priority-v3) run with the console on the settings and on the measured throughput. The curves make the day harder than planned: slower screening on the day, and a roster one lane short.

Assumed planning rule, not the airport's: every hour, enough lanes to screen the expected arrivals at 90% utilisation, at least 2 and at most 12 lanes.

Assumed: staff on call can open 2 extra lanes beyond the plan, about 10 minutes after the decision (5 to 20 on most days); an extra lane stays open at least 30 minutes; the duty manager follows 4 recommendations of GateFlow out of 5.
About 150 passengers per hour per lane (assumed modern lanes with several divesting positions).
Assumed typical configurations by ICAO type designator (one class on short haul, two or three on long haul), not airline data. Replace with the airport's seat data.

Nominal walk from the checkpoint exit: A and B are Schengen gates, C non-Schengen gates after passport control (its queue is not modelled). Long-haul flights use zone C; the others draw a zone with these shares.

Summer load factors, drawn per flight and day. With the flight list the day has about 22,000 departing passengers, about 1.35 times the average day of 2025 (11.85 million passengers, half of them departing, over 365 days): assumed peak-day factor.
Few connecting passengers cross this checkpoint (an origin-and-destination airport).
Arrival at the checkpoint = STD minus (25 min + log-normal with median 70 min), as in the demo scenario.
Connecting passengers arrive later, after their inbound flight.
Individual walking time = nominal zone time x log-normal(median 1, sigma).
Virtual queue only. As in the demo scenario; to be measured in a pilot.
More couples and families than on a normal day (leisure season).
Parties taking the assisted path (PRM and similar), as in the demo scenario.
Nobody arrives late on purpose.
Boarding closes 20 minutes before the scheduled departure, for every flight.
The system applies the closing rule to the schedule; without disruptions it matches the ground truth exactly.
No delays unless a day says otherwise (see vce-like-disrupted-day).
No gate changes unless a day says otherwise.
No unplanned lane outages unless a day says otherwise.
The flight feed never goes down unless a day says otherwise.
GateFlow defaults (priority v3 0.2.0, the virtual queue of ADR-017 and the lane recommendations of ADR-039), to be approved by the airport for this checkpoint.

Baseline A' as in ADR-022: every 5 minutes staff call the flights closing within 20 minutes. With a supervisor (@reactive, ADR-039), an extra lane opens when the queue shows more than 10 minutes and closes below 2. To replace with how this airport handles urgent passengers and long queues.
The criterion of ADR-025, to be approved by the airport.

modelLimitations: Single checkpoint. Lanes follow a planned schedule, minus unplanned outages when the scenario has them: a lane going out of service finishes its passenger first, at least one lane always stays open, and the system knows at once.

Extra lanes (policies with lane management, S8) open beyond the plan only up to the lanes the checkpoint has and the staff on call. A decision to open takes the day's delay to put a lane into service, an extra lane stays open for a minimum time, and staff go back when the plan itself needs the lane. Staff on call have no other duties in the model, and their cost is counted as extra lane-hours only. The supervisor of today's practice decides on the wait the queue shows; GateFlow recommends on a forecast of arrivals (the average of 50 other simulated days with the same flights, scaled by the arrivals of the last hour), and the duty manager follows each recommendation with the scenario's probability.
Every passenger uses the virtual queue when one is simulated: no opt-outs, no passengers without a phone or a view of the displays.

Response times and absences are drawn per party from assumed distributions. A second call does not make an absent passenger come sooner, the prepare window does not shorten response times, and a passenger who has been at the access point once answers later calls at once.
The access point never becomes a bottleneck, and the walk from the access point to the lanes is part of the response time.

Fast track (priority v2): a fast-tracked party is called next and, once its ticket is validated, goes ahead of the people waiting at the lanes who still have room under K. The fast-track entry never becomes a bottleneck of its own and needs no staff in the model.
CRITICAL passengers are flagged for staff, but staff escorts are not modelled: such passengers wait in the queue order.

Before any disruption the system's deadline equals the ground truth (boarding close from a fixed rule). Delays and gate changes, when the scenario has them, are known only once the flight feed announces them, and messages sent while the feed is down arrive when it recovers. Delays only move boarding later; passengers still arrive for the scheduled departure. A gate change affects only passengers who finish screening after it.
Staff of baseline A' learn of delays when the system does and keep using the last known times while the feed is down (no stale-data rule).
Passengers never abandon the queue, even after their flight has closed.
A group stays together: one ticket, one call, one lane, screened one person after the other. Assisted passengers always get the next free lane and are not assessed by the engine.

Baseline A' (`fifo-manual`) is an idealised staff practice: every five minutes staff call the flights closing within 20 minutes, and every passenger of those flights comes forward at once. Real practice is less systematic, so A' may overstate today's handling where it is informal, or understate it where staff watch individual passengers.
Strategic late arrivals are a fixed share in a stress-test scenario, not a behavioural response to the policy.
Tickets are issued on arrival with no kiosk or scanning delay.

The engine estimates screening time as the mean screening time per person, walking time as the nominal time of the gate zone, and the time from call to screening as the larger of the response estimate and the call-ahead time (through the fast track: the response estimate, or the time since the passenger was last at the access point when shorter).
